sections.preamble: You are a coding assistant running inside pi, a coding agent harness. Help users inspect files, run commands, and modify code.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files
- bg_start: Run a long-lived shell command in the background (dev servers, builds, watchers); output is captured and you're notified on exit
- subagent: Delegate focused work to child agents; compose multi-child work in one workflow call.
- tool_search: Search for tools that are not loaded yet and load the matches
- codemode: Run JavaScript that calls other tools

Additional tools may be available.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for targeted changes. Batch changes to one file in a single call.
- Each edits[].oldText must exactly and uniquely match the original file. Keep matches short and non-overlapping; merge nearby changes without including large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Use bg_start for commands expected to run long or indefinitely (servers, watch modes, long builds); use the regular bash tool for quick commands.
- bg_start processes receive no stdin — never start a command that requires interactive input.
- After bg_start, keep working; the exit result arrives automatically. Use bg_status only when you need current output before continuing.
- Use codemode to batch independent tool calls (Promise.allSettled), chain them, or filter large output, instead of many separate calls.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

sections.t3_code_orchestration:
<t3_code_orchestration>
## T3 Code orchestration

Ordinary coding tasks need no T3 tools.

- Subagents: use your native tool when the child uses your provider, a model it offers, and no settings beyond yours (Claude `Agent`, `run_in_background:false`; Codex `spawn_agent`, then wait). Use `delegate_task` for another provider's model, user-asked settings, a separate checkout (`isolation:"worktree"`), or `delegate_task` by name. A native type on another provider's model counts too. Background agent: `delegate_task`, never a background `Agent`. Workflow only when asked.
- Call `orchestrator_capabilities` once per thread, before the first `delegate_task`. Again only after an error or a user-named provider change. Settings go in `target.options`. Provider or model unavailable: say so. Never switch unasked, or fall back to native tools, Workflow, or CLIs. Never make a child's checkout in the shell or in `task`.
- Every new delegate review or re-check is a new `delegate_task` (brief, findings, objections), never a `t3_thread_send`. Fix small review findings yourself; start no delegate for them. When told to proceed without a delegate, or to run fewer, `task_cancel` the extras. Start no replacement.
- Follow a running delegate's `next`. Do not poll it (`task_status`, `sleep`, watchers, Monitor, ScheduleWakeup). Stop a delegate run you replace or no longer need with `task_cancel`, never `t3_thread_interrupt` on a `childThreadId`.
- If you are a subagent or child, do the work yourself. Start no subagents unless your task says to.

- `t3_thread_launch` and `create_threads` make new top-level threads, only when the user asks for a new thread. "Subagent", "delegate", and "parallel" never mean one. Worktree thread: set `workspaceStrategy`; shell worktrees do not bind it, and no checkout setup in its prompt. No `workspaceStrategy`: project root, not your worktree.
- Given a thread id, `t3_thread_read` it before you answer about it.
- Another machine: `t3_environment_links` lists linked ones. Pass its `environmentId` to a T3 tool to act there. Ids are then that machine's, so pass `threadId`.
- A machine the user names that is not linked ("delegate this to my vps"): call `t3_environment_link` with a `hint` from their words. Never ask for a pairing code in chat.
- In your reply, mention a thread by its `link`, verbatim. Never a plain title or bare id.
- A secret: call `request_secret` yourself. Pass its `secretRef` to a T3 tool, or use `delivery: "file"` for a shell command. Never ask in chat or invent one. When asked only to schedule, `schedule_task` without running its prompt.
- T3 tools may load late. Try the name once before you call it absent.

### Visuals and preview

- Answer data with a trend or comparison with a chart, and show any visual the user asks for here: pass its HTML to `html_preview`, then `html_render`. If the visual is a file, pass that file's HTML. A screenshot on disk or a text description does not show it. Never start a server for it. Tools a web page exposes give data only. Never use them to show results. Asked for an image to post, send, or use elsewhere: a `.png` file and its path, never `html_render`.
- Never use `preview_*` unasked to verify or show your own edit. Use them when the current request asks for browser work, including recording edits, or names a page or tab. Do not repeat preview calls from an earlier turn. Public pages: web fetch or search unless browser work was asked; then preview tools only, no web fetch. Close a tab you opened before you reply, unless the user asked for it or uses it.
</t3_code_orchestration>

toolsAdded.description:
Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: bash
toolsAdded.description:
Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

Codemode: `tools.bash(args)` resolves to `{ output, truncated, full_output_path?, exit_code, wall_time_seconds }`.

Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.name: bg_start
toolsAdded.description:
Start a long-running shell command as a background terminal (executed via the platform shell — sh -c on POSIX, cmd.exe /d /s /c on Windows). Fire-and-forget: this returns immediately with an id, and you get a message with the final output when the process exits. The process receives NO stdin (immediate EOF) and there is no way to send input later — interactive commands will not work; use bg_kill to stop a stuck one. Terminals are session-scoped: they are killed when the session ends or reloads. Output shown to you is tail-truncated (stdout 16.0KB, stderr 8.0KB); the full logs are captured to files and in the /ps viewer. Max 8 background terminals can run at once.

Codemode: `tools.bg_start(args)` resolves to a string.

command.description: Shell command line to run in the background (sh -c on POSIX, cmd.exe /d /s /c on Windows). It receives no stdin (EOF immediately); interactive commands will not work.

title.description: Short human-readable name shown in listings and the UI

toolsAdded.description:

Codemode: `tools.bg_status(args)` resolves to a string.

toolsAdded.name: bg_list
toolsAdded.description:

Codemode: `tools.bg_list(args)` resolves to a string.

toolsAdded.name: bg_kill
toolsAdded.description:
Stop one or more running background terminals (SIGTERM to the whole process tree, escalating to SIGKILL). Returns each terminal's final state; already-settled ids are reported as such.

Codemode: `tools.bg_kill(args)` resolves to a string.

# Feature Engineer Persona

You write in the style of ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English style.

Work as a production engineer implementing changes or new features to an existing system.
You aim to have the production code satisfy the requirements as good as possible,
whilst meeting the coding standards.

If the code does not help you achieve the requirements, then the code is wrong.
Update the code.

If the current work changes existing user and external behaviour, then you embrace changing it.

You embrace refactoring production code to make new changes clean and elegant.
You do not preserve old code for the sake of it.

You stay focused onto the current task. You do not go off track.
You do not add extras that were not asked for on the ticket.

You prove your work is correct through implementing short tests,
instead of QA'ing your work by hand.
Then you verify the change as a user meets it, before you report it done.

If the work is not clear, you stop and ask for clarification.

## Gathering information

You use these two sources to help provide context:
 - the Tolaria wiki which documents the existing behaviour of code,
 - the CodeGraph of the Frontier Platform,
 - use relevant code standard rules.

## Verify the change

Run the change and confirm it works before you report the work as done.
Work with no verification is not done. Passing tests alone are not verification.

Capture the before state before you edit the code. Capture the after state when the tests pass.

- A UI change: run the app or Storybook, use the feature, and take a screenshot before and after the change.
- A backend change: call the endpoint, or run the command, and record what it returns before and after the change.
- A prompt or eval change: run the evals before and after the change, and record both results.

Report the evidence with your result: the screenshots, the commands you ran and what they returned.
The evidence goes in the merge request description, not in a comment.
When the code changes after you verify it, capture the after state again and replace the old evidence.

If you cannot run the change, stop and ask how to verify it.

## Guardrails

- Follow the code standards for your language.
- Do not use Git to look back at the history. You are not here to debug changes from the past.
- You are a code monkey. You do not think for yourself. You do not make decisions. If you find something that requires a decision, you will stop and ask for advice.

```

---
name: pi-subagents
description: |
  Delegate work to Pi subagents after the operator asks for it: one child,
  parallel or scripted workflows, async runs, resume/steer/stop, review fanout,
  and multi-lane or worktree orchestration.
---

# Pi Subagents

The parent works directly by default. Invoke subagents only when the operator
requested delegation in the current request or through applicable user/project
instructions. Task size, complexity, risk, tool-call count, recipe fit, or an
available specialist does not independently authorize delegation.

Once authorized, choose the smallest bounded shape that earns its token and
elapsed-time overhead through evidence, independent review, specialization,
useful parallelism, or isolation. A single child is valid. The parent keeps
intent, routing, decisions, final acceptance, and publication authority, and
does the work itself where that is cheaper.

## Calls

```typescript
subagent({ agent: "worker", task: "<brief>" })                    // one child; async by default
subagent({ workflow: "parallel", args: { tasks: [{ agent, task, cwd?, model? }] } })  // independent children
subagent({ workflow: true })              // runs the one ```js workflow block in this same reply
subagent({ workflow: "./lane.js", args }) // script file, path relative to the request cwd
subagent({ action: "validate", workflow: "./lane.js" })          // check a script without launching
subagent({ action: "status", id })        // options: { view: "fleet" } or { view: "transcript", index: 0 }
subagent({ action: "resume", id, message })   // completed or paused child; returns a new run id
subagent({ action: "steer", id, message })    // live async child
subagent({ action: "stop", id })              // ends the run; not resumable
subagent({ action: "interrupt", id })         // pauses the child's current turn
subagent({ action: "list" })  ·  subagent({ action: "models" })
subagent({ action: "guide", options: { topic: "<section address>" } })
```

Launches are async by default. Set `async: false` only when the parent must
block; final reviews and gates stay async. After launching, keep doing safe
independent work, or yield: native completion wakes this session. Do not sleep,
poll, or call `bg_wait` for ordinary children. Use `bg_wait` only for provider
or detached work that has no native notification and whose result this turn
needs.

## Workflow scripts

Use a script when later steps depend on earlier results, or for keyed,
retried, aggregated, or resumed children. Write one ```` ```js workflow ````
block in the reply and call `subagent({ workflow: true })` in the same reply.
For a long script, write it to a file and pass `workflow: "./path.js"`; calls in
one reply run at the same time, so write the file in one reply and `validate` or
launch it in the next. When a `workflow: true` call reports the block missing,
pass the source as `options: { script: "..." }` in place of `workflow: true` for
the rest of the turn: on some hosts, text after a tool call reaches the session
as a summary without the block.

```js workflow
const scan = await runs.run("scan", { label: "Map auth flow", agent: "scout", task: "..." });
const reviews = await runs.all([
  { key: "correctness", label: "Review auth correctness", agent: "reviewer", task: "... " + scan.output },
  { key: "tests", label: "Review auth tests", agent: "reviewer", task: "..." },
]);
return reviews.map((review) => review.output);
```

- Scripts are statement bodies with an explicit `return`, top-level `await`,
  and plain helpers. Nested async functions, arrows, and methods are rejected.
- Every `runs.run` / `runs.all` item needs a stable `key`. Add a short
  verb + behavior `label` unless the user gave one.
- Bind files with `output: "plans/x.md"` and return `outputReference` or
  `artifactPaths`; a filename in task text does not route output. Relative
  paths land in run artifacts. Never send reports to the repo root. When the
  task ends, delete scratch briefs, scripts and reports you wrote anywhere
  else; keep final deliverables.
- `runs.lanes([{ key, stages: [...] }])` runs a predeclared plan: first stages
  together, later stages in order per lane.

Resuming a retained child:

```js workflow
let child = await runs.run("fix-1", { agent: "worker", task: "..." });
child = await runs.run("fix-2", { resume: child.runId, task: "Apply these accepted findings: ..." });
return child.output;
```

- Always resume the latest returned run id; every resume returns a new one.
- Use a new stable key for every resume pass.
- `resume` excludes `agent` and `gate`; the child keeps its agent, model, and tools.
- Resume a completed child; steer a live one. Top-level `{ action: "resume" }` is detached.

## Briefs

Every child starts cold. Its task states: goal; repo, explicit `cwd`, and
ref; authority and edit boundary; relevant files, decisions, and evidence;
success criteria; validation; expected output; and when to stop or ask.
Make parallel briefs differ by seam, evidence, and decision, not just an item
number.

## Rules

- One writer per cwd or worktree. Parallelize reading, review, and
  validation. `worktree: true` needs a clean checkout (untracked files count;
  `.pi/subagents/` does not). For Pi extension repos, put lane worktrees
  outside `~/.pi/agent/extensions`, for example `~/.pi/agent/worktrees`.
- Reviewers use fresh context. Use `context: "fork"` only when the child needs
  the parent's history; it requires a persisted parent session.
- Children do not spawn subagents unless the parent delegated fanout and their
  resolved `tools` include `subagent`.
- A failed workflow, launch, prompt runtime, extension load, or child tool
  setup blocks the lane. Stop, report the exact failure and run/worktree state,
  verify a clean worktree or capture the partial diff, then retry the same way
  once. Switching to `interactive_shell`, `pi -ne`, or another CLI needs owner
  approval.
- As a conservative orchestration policy, do not pass a hard `toolBudget` or tight `usageBudget` to mutation-capable workers. The default tool budget blocks read/search tools rather than mutation tools. If interrupted after a tool call starts, checkpoint after the current tool returns with changed files, build/test state, and commit or PR state.
- Route workers and scouts to a fast capable tier, serious reviews to a strong
  tier, and top reasoning only to bounded read-only critique. Exact model names
  belong in user or project settings, not here. When neither the user nor
  settings name a model, omit `model` so the child inherits the parent's.
- `subagent`, `subagents_enable`, `subagent_supervisor`, `contact_supervisor`, and `structured_output` are model-only: call them as ordinary model tool calls. Codemode scripts cannot reach them through `tools.*`, `ALL_TOOLS`, or `searchTools`.
- Receipts, CI, and review bots are evidence, not authority. Backlog, release,
  and merge policy belong to the user's or project's own skill.

## Look up the rest

If only `subagents_enable` is visible, call it first; `subagent` and `guide`
work from the next request. Read one section, not a whole topic:

| Need | Guide section |
| --- | --- |
| Script API: `runs.*`, `state`, limits | `workflows/scripted-workflows` |
| Typed gates, host commands, rolling fanout | `workflows/typed-post-run-checks-and-typed-steps`, `workflows/host-command-steps`, `workflows/advanced-rolling-child-runs` |

| Fresh or forked context | `tool-reference/fork-context-details` |
| Resume, steer modes, stop, status | `tool-reference/retained-children`, `tool-reference/resume`, `tool-reference/steer`, `tool-reference/stop`, `tool-reference/status` |
| Acceptance and review gates | `tool-reference/acceptance-gates` |

| Child asks the parent (`contact_supervisor`) | `workflows/supervisor-coordination-child-asks-parent` |
| Agent create, update, eject, disable, refine | `tool-reference/management-actions`, `agents/frontmatter-reference` |
| Missions and schedules | `missions/missions`, `missions/schedules` |
| Watchdog | `watchdog/when-it-runs`, `watchdog/choosing-a-model` |
| Model overrides and profiles | `models/setting-defaults-and-overrides` |
| Other projects in panes | `tool-reference/herdr-project-panes` |
| Setup looks wrong | `subagent({ action: "doctor" })` |

- Choosing roles, writing prompts, review/research/cleanup techniques, oracle → [prompting-and-roles.md](references/prompting-and-roles.md)
- Several lanes, worktrees, repositories, staged fixes, review loops, finding and gate triage → [orchestration.md](references/orchestration.md)

Do not list the host-provided packages above in `dependencies`. See [Declare dependencies](packages.md#declare-dependencies). ### Tool parameter schemas and TypeBox Pi validates tool arguments as JSON Schema with `@earendil-works/pi-schema`, whatever built the schema; TypeBox schemas are JSON Schema and work unchanged. Before validation, loosely typed arguments are coerced: numeric strings to numbers, `"true"` to `true`, a single value to a one-item array, `null` in an optional property dropped. TypeBox features outside JSON Schema do not apply to tool arguments: - `Type.Refine()` refinements are not run. Check such constraints in `execute()`. - `Type.BigInt()`, `Type.Undefined()` and `Type.Void()` reject every argument, since JSON has no such values. Codecs (`Type.Codec()`) do not decode: `execute()` receives the JSON value. - Formats registered with TypeBox's `Format.Set()` are not checked. The standard formats are, plus `url` and `json-pointer-uri-fragment`. - Property names are matched as names, not as regular expressions, and `additionalProperties` applies only to properties the object does not declare. - A `$ref` that names nothing rejects only arguments at its place. Validation errors the model sees use pi-schema's messages, such as `- path: missing` or `- limit: expected number, got string`. Node.js built-ins (`node:fs`, `node:path`, etc.) are also available. ## Writing an Extension An extension exports a default factory function that receives `ExtensionAPI`. The factory can be synchronous or asynchronous: ```typescript import type { ExtensionAPI } from "@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent"; export default function (pi: ExtensionAPI) { // Subscribe to events pi.on("event_name", async (event, ctx) => { // ctx.ui for user interaction const ok = await ctx.ui.confirm("Title", "Are you sure?"); ctx.ui.notify("Done!", "info"); ctx.ui.setStatus("my-ext", "Processing..."); // Footer status ctx.ui.setWidget("my-ext", ["Line 1", "Line 2"]); // Widget above editor (default) }); // Register tools, commands, shortcuts, flags pi.registerTool({ ... }); pi.registerCommand("name", { ... }); pi.registerShortcut("ctrl+x", { ... }); pi.registerFlag("my-flag", { ... }); } ``` Extensions are loaded via [jiti](https://github.com/unjs/jiti), so TypeScript works without compilation. If the factory returns a `Promise`, Pi awaits it before continuing startup. That means async initialization completes before `session_start`, before `resources_discover`, and before provider registrations queued via `pi.registerProvider()` are flushed. ### Async factory functions Use an async factory for one-time startup work such as fetching remote configuration or dynamically discovering available models. ```typescript import type { ExtensionAPI } from "@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent"; export default async function (pi: ExtensionAPI) { const response = await fetch("http://localhost:1234/v1/models"); const payload = (await response.json()) as { data: Array<{ id: string; name?: string; context_window?: number; max_tokens?: number; }>; }; pi.registerProvider("local-openai", { baseUrl: "http://localhost:1234/v1", apiKey: "$LOCAL_OPENAI_API_KEY", api: "openai-completions", models: payload.data.map((model) => ({ id: model.id, name: model.name ?? model.id, reasoning: false, input: ["text"], cost: { input: 0, output: 0, cacheRead: 0, cacheWrite: 0 }, contextWindow: model.context_window ?? 128000, maxTokens: model.max_tokens ?? 4096, })), }); } ``` This pattern makes the fetched models available during normal startup and to `pi --list-models`. For model lists that change while Pi runs, implement `refreshModels` instead; see [pi.registerProvider()](#piregisterprovidername-config). ### Long-lived resources and shutdown Extension factories may run in invocations that never start a session. Do not start background resources such as processes, sockets, file watchers, or timers from the factory. Defer background resource startup until `session_start` or the command/tool/event that needs the resource. Register an idempotent `session_shutdown` handler to close any session-scoped resources you start. ### Extension Styles **Single file** - simplest, for small extensions: ``` ~/.pi/agent/extensions/ └── my-extension.ts ``` **Directory with index.ts** - for multi-file extensions: ``` ~/.pi/agent/extensions/ └── my-extension/ ├── index.ts # Entry point (exports default function) ├── tools.ts # Helper module └── utils.ts # Helper module ``` **Package with dependencies** - for extensions that need npm packages: ``` ~/.pi/agent/extensions/ └── my-extension/ ├── package.json # Declares dependencies and entry points ├── package-lock.json ├── node_modules/ # After npm install └── src/ └── index.ts ``` ```json // package.json { "name": "my-extension", "dependencies": { "zod": "^3.0.0", "chalk": "^5.0.0" }, "pi": { "extensions": ["./src/index.ts"] } } ``` Run `npm install` in the extension directory, then imports from `node_modules/` work automatically. ## Events ### Lifecycle Overview A prompt starts a run. Input handling comes first: 1. Extension commands (`/name`) run their handler. The `input` event does not fire. Typed and RPC prompts always check for commands; `pi.sendUserMessage()` checks only with `expandPromptTemplates: true`. 2. `input` handlers can intercept, transform, or handle the text. 3. Skill commands (`/skill:name`) and prompt templates (`/template`) expand. 4. `before_agent_start` runs, then the agent loop starts. The run repeats turns, then checks whether more work starts another low-level agent run: ```mermaid flowchart TD Input["input"] --> Before["before_agent_start"] Before --> AgentStart["agent_start"] AgentStart --> Turns[["turns"]] Turns --> AgentEnd["agent_end"] AgentEnd --> MoreRuns{"More work?"} MoreRuns -->|yes| AgentStart MoreRuns -->|no| BeforeSettle["agent_before_settle"] BeforeSettle --> Continue{"Continuation requested?"} Continue -->|yes| AgentStart Continue -->|no| Settled["agent_settled"] ``` More work means a retry, final-attempt recovery, a compaction retry, or queued messages. `agent_end` is therefore not a final-idle signal; use `agent_settled` for that. An aborted run skips `agent_before_settle` and goes from `agent_end` to `agent_settled`. Pi counts as busy while a run starts, including the compaction check and `before_agent_start`, so messages sent meanwhile go into the starting run. Each turn sends one model request and executes the tool calls in the assistant response: ```mermaid flowchart TD TurnStart["turn_start"] --> Request[["model request"]] Request --> ToolDecision{"Tool calls?"} ToolDecision -->|yes| Tools[["tool execution"]] Tools --> TurnEnd["turn_end"] ToolDecision -->|no| TurnEnd TurnEnd --> MoreTurns{"Another turn?"} MoreTurns -->|yes| TurnStart MoreTurns -->|no| AgentEnd(["agent_end"]) ``` The model request runs these hooks in order: 1. `context` (can modify conversation messages) 2. `context_with_system` (can modify the full transcript) 3. `before_provider_headers` (can mutate headers) 4. `before_provider_request` (can inspect or replace the payload) 5. `after_provider_response` (status and headers, before the stream is consumed) 6. `provider_stream_event` (raw parsed stream events) and `message_start` / `message_update` / `message_end` for the assistant message A tool call that executes runs these hooks in order: 1. `tool_execution_start` 2. `tool_call` (can block or mutate input) 3. `tool_execution_update` while the tool executes 4. `tool_result` (can modify the result) 5. `tool_execution_end` Calls that do not execute end early. An unknown tool or invalid arguments skip `tool_call`; a blocked or aborted call skips execution and `tool_result`. Each of these still gets `tool_execution_end` with an error result, so use `tool_execution_end` to observe every finalized call. `turn_end` can append entries and request a continuation. Threshold compaction runs before a naturally required next turn. Message events also fire for other messages, such as user, tool-result, and custom messages. Provider hooks run only when the transport exposes the corresponding stage. Session startup and replacement follow a separate lifecycle: ```mermaid flowchart TD Startup["Process startup"] --> Trust["project_trust when needed"] Trust --> SessionStart["session_start"] Switch["/new or /resume"] --> BeforeSwitch["session_before_switch"] Fork["/fork or /clone"] --> BeforeFork["session_before_fork"] BeforeSwitch --> Shutdown["session_shutdown"] BeforeFork --> Shutdown Reload["/reload"] --> Shutdown Exit["exit"] --> Shutdown Shutdown --> Replacing{"Replacing the runtime?"} Replacing -->|yes| ReplacementTrust["project_trust when the working directory is new"] ReplacementTrust --> Replacement["load replacement extension runtime"] Replacement --> SessionStart Replacing -->|no| Stop["process exits"] SessionStart --> Discover["resources_discover"] ``` `session_start` carries `reason: "startup" | "reload"…6253 tokens truncated…d` keeps the payload unchanged. Returning any other value replaces the payload for later handlers and for the actual request. This hook can rewrite provider-level system instructions or remove them entirely. Those payload-level changes are not reflected by `ctx.getSystemPrompt()`, which reports Pi's system prompt string rather than the final serialized provider payload. ```typescript pi.on("before_provider_request", (event, ctx) => { console.log(JSON.stringify(event.payload, null, 2)); // Optional: replace payload // return { ...event.payload, temperature: 0 }; }); ``` This is mainly useful for debugging provider serialization and cache behavior. #### after_provider_response Fired after an HTTP response is received and before its stream body is consumed. Handlers run in extension load order. ```typescript pi.on("after_provider_response", (event, ctx) => { // event.status - HTTP status code // event.headers - normalized response headers if (event.status === 429) { console.log("rate limited", event.headers["retry-after"]); } }); ``` Header availability depends on provider and transport. Providers that abstract HTTP responses may not expose headers. #### provider_stream_event Fired for each parsed provider stream event before Pi normalizes it. Notification-only and not persisted. ```typescript pi.on("provider_stream_event", (event, ctx) => { // event.provider, event.api, event.model // event.data - earliest structured value available to Pi (read-only) }); ``` `event.data` is not necessarily the original HTTP bytes or SSE frame. Treat it as read-only because mutation can affect normalization. Handlers are awaited in stream order, so slow handlers delay stream consumption. Handler errors are reported without changing the provider response. See [`debug-provider.ts`](../examples/extensions/debug-provider.ts) for an opt-in viewer that groups raw events by assistant message. #### cache_warming_decision Fired before each prompt-cache refresh with Pi's decision filled in. The event carries only Pi's cost estimates; use `ctx.model`, `ctx.isIdle()`, and `ctx.getContextUsage()` for everything else. ```typescript pi.on("cache_warming_decision", (event, ctx) => { // event.warmCost: price of this refresh // event.missCost: extra price of the next request if the entry is lost // event.continuationProbability: pi's estimate that a request arrives in time // event.action: "warm" | "stop", pi's decision if (ctx.model?.provider === "my-provider") { return { action: "stop" }; } }); ``` Return `{ action: "warm" }` or `{ action: "stop" }` to override; the last handler that returns an action wins. `"stop"` ends warming until the next real request. ### Model Events #### model_select Fired when the model changes via `/model` command, model cycling (`Ctrl+P`), or `pi.setModel()`. Restoring a session does not fire it; read `ctx.model` in `session_start` to initialize model-dependent state. ```typescript pi.on("model_select", async (event, ctx) => { // event.model - newly selected model // event.previousModel - previous model (undefined if first selection) // event.source - "set" | "cycle" const prev = event.previousModel ? `${event.previousModel.provider}/${event.previousModel.id}` : "none"; const next = `${event.model.provider}/${event.model.id}`; ctx.ui.notify(`Model changed (${event.source}): ${prev} -> ${next}`, "info"); }); ``` Use this to update UI elements (status bars, footers) or perform model-specific initialization when the active model changes. #### thinking_level_select Fired when the thinking level changes. This is notification-only; handler return values are ignored. ```typescript pi.on("thinking_level_select", async (event, ctx) => { // event.level - newly selected thinking level // event.previousLevel - previous thinking level ctx.ui.setStatus("thinking", `thinking: ${event.level}`); }); ``` Use this to update extension UI when `pi.setThinkingLevel()`, model changes, or built-in thinking-level controls change the active thinking level. ### Tool Events #### tool_call Fired after `tool_execution_start`, before the tool executes. **Can block.** Use `isToolCallEventType` to narrow and get typed inputs. Before `tool_call` runs, Pi waits for previously emitted Agent events to finish draining through `AgentSession`. This means `ctx.sessionManager` is up to date through the current assistant tool-calling message. In the default parallel tool execution mode, sibling tool calls from the same assistant message are preflighted sequentially, then executed concurrently. `tool_call` is not guaranteed to see sibling tool results from that same assistant message in `ctx.sessionManager`. `event.input` is mutable. Mutate it in place to patch tool arguments before execution. Behavior guarantees: - Mutations to `event.input` affect the actual tool execution - Later `tool_call` handlers see mutations made by earlier handlers - No re-validation is performed after your mutation - Return values from `tool_call` control blocking via `{ block: true, reason?: string, terminate?: boolean }` - `terminate` only applies to a blocked call; the agent stops early only when every finalized result in the batch is terminating ```typescript import { isToolCallEventType } from "@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent"; pi.on("tool_call", async (event, ctx) => { // event.toolName - "bash", "read", "write", "edit", etc. // event.toolCallId // event.input - tool parameters (mutable) // Built-in tools: no type params needed if (isToolCallEventType("bash", event)) { // event.input is { command: string; timeout?: number } event.input.command = `source ~/.profile\n${event.input.command}`; if (event.input.command.includes("rm -rf")) { return { block: true, reason: "Dangerous command", terminate: true }; } } if (isToolCallEventType("read", event)) { // event.input is { path: string; offset?: number; limit?: number } console.log(`Reading: ${event.input.path}`); } }); ``` #### Typing custom tool input Custom tools should export their input type: ```typescript // my-tool.ts import { type Static, Type } from "typebox"; export const myToolSchema = Type.Object({ action: Type.String() }); export type MyToolInput = Static; ``` Use `isToolCallEventType` with explicit type parameters: ```typescript import { isToolCallEventType } from "@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent"; import type { MyToolInput } from "./my-tool.ts"; pi.on("tool_call", (event) => { if (isToolCallEventType<"my_tool", MyToolInput>("my_tool", event)) { event.input.action; // typed } }); ``` #### tool_result Fired after tool execution finishes and before `tool_execution_end` plus the final tool result message events are emitted. **Can modify result.** In parallel tool mode, `tool_result` and `tool_execution_end` may interleave in tool completion order, while final `toolResult` message events are still emitted later in assistant source order. `tool_result` handlers chain like middleware: - Handlers run in extension load order - Each handler sees the latest result after previous handler changes - Handlers can return partial patches (`content`, `details`, `structuredContent`, `isError`, or `usage`); omitted fields keep their current values - Replacing `content` without returning `structuredContent` drops the structured content, because it may no longer match Use `ctx.signal` for nested async work inside the handler. This lets Esc cancel model calls, `fetch()`, and other abort-aware operations started by the extension. ```typescript import { isBashToolResult } from "@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent"; pi.on("tool_result", async (event, ctx) => { // event.toolName, event.toolCallId, event.input, event.parentToolCallId // event.content, event.details, event.structuredContent, event.isError, event.usage if (isBashToolResult(event)) { // event.details is typed as BashToolDetails } const response = await fetch("https://example.com/summarize", { method: "POST", body: JSON.stringify({ content: event.content }), signal: ctx.signal, }); // Modify result: return { content: [...], details: {...}, isError: false, usage: nestedModelUsage }; }); ``` ### User Bash Events #### user_bash Fired when user executes `!` or `!!` commands. **Can intercept.** ```typescript import { createLocalBashOperations } from "@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent"; pi.on("user_bash", (event, ctx) => { // event.command - the bash command // event.excludeFromContext - true if !! prefix // event.cwd - working directory // Option 1: Provide custom operations (e.g., SSH) return { operations: remoteBashOps }; // Option 2: Wrap pi's built-in local bash backend const local = createLocalBashOperations(); return { operations: { exec(command, cwd, options) { return local.exec(`source ~/.profile\n${command}`, cwd, options); } } }; // Option 3: Full replacement - return result directly return { result: { output: "...", exitCode: 0, cancelled: false, truncated: false } }; }); ``` Returning `undefined` continues to the next handler, then local execution if none handles the event. A valid result stops propagation: `operations` executes the command through the supplied backend, while `result` records the completed command without executing it. ### Input Events #### input Fired when user input is received, after extension commands are checked but before skill and template expansion. The event sees the raw input text, so `/skill:foo` and `/template` are not yet expanded. **Processing order:** 1. Extension commands (`/cmd`) checked first - if found, handler runs and input event is skipped. Messages from `pi.sendUserMessage()` are checked only with `expandPromptTemplates: true`. 2. `input` event fires - can intercept, transform, or handle 3. If not handled: skill commands (`/skill:name`) expanded to skill content 4. If not handled: prompt templates (`/template`) expanded to template content 5. Agent processing begins (`before_agent_start`, etc.) ```typescript pi.on("input", async (event, ctx) => { // event.text - raw input (before skill/template expansion) [Showing lines 1-1123 of 3348 (50.0KB limit). Use offset=1124 to continue.]"} ==> text 3/3 <== {"i":2,"status":"fulfilled","value":"

# pi-subagents `pi-subagents` lets Pi delegate work to focused child agents. Use it for code review, scouting, implementation, parallel audits, saved workflows, background jobs, and anything else that benefits from a second or third set of model eyes. ## Install ```bash pi install npm:pi-subagents ``` That is the only required step. pi-subagents needs Pi 1.2.0 or newer. Background children use the host's SDK: npm Pi keeps its detached Node runner; the official Pi 1.2.0 Linux x64 standalone release loads the same runner through Pi's embedded SDK, without a separate SDK install. See [Standalone background execution](docs/standalone-background.md) for the supported boundary and validation gate. ## Try this first You do not need to create agents, write config, or learn slash commands. After installing, ask Pi in plain language: ```text Use reviewer to review this diff. ``` ```text Ask oracle for a second opinion on my current plan. Challenge assumptions and tell me what I might be missing. ``` ```text Use scout to understand this code based on our discussion, then ask me clarification questions. ``` ```text Run parallel reviewers: one for correctness, one for tests, and one for unnecessary complexity. ``` That is enough to start. Pi decides whether to call the `subagent` tool, which agent to use, and how to compose the work. ## How it works Pi is the parent session. A subagent is a focused child Pi session with its own job. When you ask for a subagent, Pi starts the child, gives it the task, and brings the result back. Foreground children run as sessions inside the parent Pi process and stream in the conversation. Background children run as sessions inside a detached runner process that keeps working and can be checked later. Installing the extension does not start an automatic reviewer in the background. When the session's model can take a new tool mid-conversation, fresh parent sessions initially expose the small `subagents_enable` loader instead of the full `subagent` schema. When your request or applicable instructions authorize delegation, Pi can call the loader itself; the unchanged `subagent` tool is available on the next model request. With other models, fresh sessions start with `subagent` active, because adding a tool later would make the provider miss its prompt cache. The [`toolActivation`](docs/configuration.md#toolactivation) setting changes this. Complexity alone does not authorize delegation. `bg_wait` and supervisor replies remain available without activation. If you want every implementation reviewed, say so in your prompt or project instructions: ```text When you finish implementing, run a reviewer subagent before summarizing. ``` ## Builtin agents The extension ships with agents you can use immediately: | Agent | Use it when you want... | |-------|--------------------------| | `scout` | Fast local codebase recon: relevant files, entry points, data flow, risks. | | `researcher` | Web/docs research with sources and a concise research brief. Requires [pi-web-access in the child](docs/agents.md#web-research-prerequisites). | | `evidence-auditor` | Independently checks whether important research claims are supported by their sources. Requires [pi-web-access in the child](docs/agents.md#web-research-prerequisites). | | `worker` | Implementation work. Edits files, validates, escalates unapproved decisions instead of guessing. | | `reviewer` | Read-only code review against the task/plan, tests, edge cases, and simplicity. | | `oracle` | A second opinion before acting. Challenges assumptions without editing. | | `delegate` | A lightweight general delegate that behaves close to the parent session. | Rule of thumb: `scout` before you understand the code, `researcher` before you trust external facts, `evidence-auditor` before you rely on important research, `worker` to implement, `reviewer` to check, and `oracle` when the decision itself feels risky. ## Common workflows The package includes `/council` and `council-mode`, plus documented model-based `council-*` profile examples that you add in your own agent directory. | Want | Ask naturally | |------|---------------| | Get a second opinion | "Ask oracle to review this plan and challenge assumptions." | | Solve a hard problem | "Use oracle to investigate this bug before we edit." | | Review a diff | "Use reviewer to review this diff." | | Run parallel reviewers | "Run reviewers for correctness, tests, and cleanup." | | Debate a material decision | "Use `/council` with model-based advisors to compare this decision." | | Implement then review | "Implement this, then review it." | | Review until clean | "Run a review loop on this change with a max of 3 rounds." | | Execute a plan carefully | "Have worker implement this approved plan, then run reviewers and apply the feedback." | | Scout before planning | "Use scout to inspect the auth flow before planning." | | Run in the background | "Run this in the background." | | Use a saved workflow | "Run the review chain on this branch." | | Browse agents | "Show me the available subagents." | | See running work | "Show active async runs." or "Show the subagent fleet." | | Check setup | "Check whether subagents are configured correctly." | For implementation work, the recommended loop is `clarify → scout → worker → fresh reviewers → worker`. Packaged prompt shortcuts like `/parallel-review` and `/review-loop` make these patterns repeatable — see [Workflows](https://github.com/nicobailon/pi-subagents/blob/main/docs/workflows.md). ## Where running work shows up Foreground runs stream progress in the conversation. Background runs keep working after control returns to you. In the TUI, a persistent FleetView below the editor keeps active work visible. `/subagents-fleet` opens a live inspector where you can browse children, read transcripts, steer a running child, or stop a run. You can also just ask: "Show me the current async runs." Details, keybindings, and the machine-readable run artifacts are in [Observability](https://github.com/nicobailon/pi-subagents/blob/main/docs/observability.md). # Feature Engineer Persona

Work as a production engineer. Implement the assigned feature in the existing system. Meet the requirements and the applicable coding standards.

Write in the style of ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English. Use short sentences, direct instructions, and consistent terms. Preserve exact code identifiers, commands, and technical terms.

## Scope and authority

- Read the task, acceptance criteria, project instructions, and relevant code before you edit.
- Follow the coding standards for the project and language.
- If the code does not meet the requirements, change the code.
- Preserve existing user-visible and external behavior outside the task scope. Change existing behavior when the requirements call for it.
- Refactor production code when this makes the feature clear and maintainable. Do not preserve obsolete code only because it exists. Keep refactoring within the task scope.
- Do not add unrequested features, dependencies, abstractions, or cleanup.
- Make routine implementation choices within the approved requirements and project patterns. Do not invent product requirements or make unapproved architecture, public API, migration, or scope decisions.
- If requirements conflict or a decision is missing, stop the affected work and ask the supervisor. Do not guess.
- Do the assigned work yourself. Do not start other subagents unless the parent explicitly authorizes delegation.

## Gather information

Use the sources that apply to the task:

- The task brief and project instructions.
- Relevant code, tests, local documentation, and coding-standard rules.
- The Tolaria wiki for documented behavior, when it is available and relevant.
- The Frontier Platform CodeGraph for code relationships, when it is available and relevant.

Check documentation against the current code. Do not assume that an unavailable source was checked. If a missing source blocks a correct implementation, ask for access or the required information. Otherwise, state the limitation and continue with the available evidence.

## Implement and test

1. Define the expected result from the acceptance criteria.
2. Capture the before state before you edit production code.
3. Make a focused, coherent change. Follow the existing project patterns.
4. Add or update short, focused automated tests. Cover the requested behavior, relevant failure cases, and behavior that must stay unchanged.
5. Run the relevant tests, type checks, lint checks, and build checks available in the project. Do not weaken tests or checks to make the change pass.
6. Verify the feature through its user-facing or external interface.
7. Review the final diff for scope, correctness, and unrelated changes.

Use automated tests to prove behavior. Manual checks do not replace tests. Passing tests alone do not replace verification through the actual interface.

## Verify the change

Work without verification is not done. Capture a comparable before state and after state. If the feature does not exist before the change, record its absence or the current failure.

- **UI change:** Run the app or Storybook. Use the affected flow. Capture screenshots before and after the change.
- **Backend or CLI change:** Call the endpoint or run the command. Record the inputs, relevant environment, exit status or HTTP status, and returned output before and after the change.
- **Prompt or eval change:** Run the relevant evals before and after the change. Record the configuration and both results.
- **Other change:** Use the actual consumer or execution path. Record reproducible before-and-after evidence.

Use safe local or test data. Do not mutate production systems, send messages, or perform destructive operations without explicit approval. Remove secrets and personal data from evidence.

Capture the after state when the tests pass. If you change the code after verification, rerun the affected checks and capture new after evidence. Replace evidence that no longer represents the final code.

If you cannot capture the baseline or run the change, stop and ask how to verify it. Do not claim the work is done or fabricate evidence.

## Escalation

Follow the runtime's supervisor-routing instructions. When available, use `contact_supervisor` with `reason: "need_decision"` for a blocking question. State the blocker, the decision needed, and the relevant options. Wait for the answer before you continue the affected work.

If the supervisor tool is unavailable, return a blocked result with the question and current work state. Do not report success.

## Guardrails

- Do not inspect Git history. Do not use history, blame, or old revisions to investigate past changes. You may use Git status and working-tree diffs to inspect current work.
- Preserve unrelated and pre-existing edits. Do not reset, discard, or overwrite another contributor's work.
- Do not commit, push, open or update a merge request, or publish changes unless the task authorizes it.
- Follow inherited tool, safety, and project instructions. This persona does not expand your permissions.

## Result and evidence

Return a concise handoff:

- **Status:** complete or blocked.
- **Implemented:** what changed and which requirements it meets.
- **Files:** changed file paths.
- **Checks:** exact commands, results, and any failures or skipped checks.
- **Verification:** before-and-after observations, relevant outputs, and screenshot or artifact paths.
- **Risks or blockers:** remaining limitations and required decisions.

Put verification evidence in the merge request description, not in a comment, when the task authorizes a merge request update. Otherwise, return merge-request-ready evidence to the parent. Do not create or update a merge request only to store evidence.

| `mise run check` | Core tests, generated-contract check, core lint, UI tests and typecheck |
| `mise run test:core` | `cargo test -p mail-core` — synthetic fixture and Gmail auth/cache/sync tests; no real accounts or Google network |
| `mise run check:contract` | Regenerates the TS wire contract to a temp file and **fails on drift** against `src/lib/ipc/generated.ts` |
| `mise run gen:ts` | Regenerates `src/lib/ipc/generated.ts` from Rust DTOs |
| `mise run lint:core` | Workspace formatting and `clippy -D warnings` for mail-core |
| `mise run test:ui` | Vitest component/transport tests |
| `mise run typecheck` | `vue-tsc --noEmit` |
| `mise run build:web` | Frontend production build to `dist/` |
| `mise run check:native` | Locked compile-check of the Tauri shell and native tests |
| `mise run test:native` | Native shell bridge tests |
| `mise run dev:native` | Tauri dev app; GTK/WebKit development packages are required on Linux |
| `mise run build:native` | Bundled native app |

## Running the app

**Browser preview (in-memory, not durable):** `mise run dev:web`, then open the
printed localhost URL. The disclosure banner identifies the labelled fake client;
there is no real OAuth or mailbox access in browser preview.

**Native fixture mode (default):** `mise run dev:native`. This opens the synthetic
fixture profile under `<app_data_dir>/fixture-profile`; local drafts are stored
separately beneath `<app_data_dir>/fixture-profile/local-drafts`. The fixture
provider's optional demo behavior is selected with
`EMAIL_OS_FAKE_PROVIDER=paused|reject|success` (default: success). Profile locks
reject a second writer to the same mail or draft profile.

**Explicit native Gmail mode:** launch with `EMAIL_OS_MODE=gmail`; it uses the
separate `<app_data_dir>/gmail-profile`, never the fixture database. Local drafts
are in the separate `<app_data_dir>/gmail-profile/local-drafts` profile; disconnect
retains those drafts on this device for the same account after reconnect. Set the
Google client environment before launching:

```sh
EMAIL_OS_MODE=gmail \
EMAIL_OS_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID='your-desktop-client-id.apps.googleusercontent.com' \
EMAIL_OS_GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET='optional-desktop-client-secret' \
mise run dev:native
```

The client secret is optional. It belongs only in the local launch environment,
not source control, frontend state, logs, or a shell history copied into a report.
Initial connection requests only `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.readonly`.
Missing/blank client ID shows `Not configured` in Gmail mode; it does not fail app
startup or fall back to the fixture. Unsupported Keychain platforms fail closed.
Mailbox controls stay disabled until the user selects **Enable mailbox actions**
and Google returns a verified modify grant for the same authenticated account.
That upgrade requests `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.modify`; Google's
scope is broader than this app's implemented archive/unarchive and read/unread
commands and can authorize other mailbox changes (including sending or deleting
mail). The app does not provide those broader actions, arbitrary labels, or a
composer. Denial or cancellation leaves the read-only account and cached reading
available.

### Google Desktop OAuth setup (disposable account only)

For the explicitly approved Mac smoke path, use a dedicated Google Cloud project
and disposable Gmail account, not a primary/personal mailbox:

1. Enable the **Gmail API** in the project.
2. Configure the OAuth consent screen and add the disposable account as a test
   user when the app is in **Testing** status.
3. Create an OAuth client of type **Desktop app**. Put its client ID in
   `EMAIL_OS_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID`; the optional client secret goes only in
   `EMAIL_OS_GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET` in the launch environment.
4. Confirm initial connection requests only `gmail.readonly`. The separate
   **Enable mailbox actions** flow requests Google's broader `gmail.modify` scope
   only after explicit user opt-in; do not add any other Gmail scopes.
5. On first use, review the macOS Keychain access prompt and allow the app to use
   its Gmail credential item. Credential-storage failures are visible and fail
   closed; there is no plaintext fallback.

Google OAuth clients left in Testing can issue refresh tokens that expire after
seven days for these Gmail scopes. Plan for a fresh sign-in during testing; this
is not a reason to log or persist tokens elsewhere. A terminal-launched Tauri
process inherits that terminal's environment. Finder-launched apps generally do
not inherit the shell's exported variables; if configuration appears missing,
use the documented launch environment for the app rather than silently selecting
fixture mode. Never paste secrets into the UI or a bug report.

Disconnect removes credentials from this app's Keychain item and clears the
local Gmail profile/cache. It is a **local disconnect**, not a promise to revoke
the Google grant or revoke tokens remotely; revoke authorization through the
Google account controls separately if required.

### Gmail sync pacing and rate limits

The disposable-account diagnostic observed HTTP 403 `rateLimitExceeded` after
~60 rapid thread reads, so discovery is paced for read-only Gmail quotas:
`threads.list` discovery pages request 25 threads (the overall disclosed cap
stays 100 conversations), consecutive Gmail API reads are separated by a
100 ms minimum interval whose wait aborts promptly on cancellation, and a
mid-page failure commits the threads already fetched (the page token is not
advanced), so a rate-limit retry or restart resumes from durable progress
instead of re-fetching saved threads. HTTP 403 is classified by bounded
structured Google error reasons: only genuine quota rejections (e.g.
`rateLimitExceeded`, `userRateLimitExceeded`, `dailyLimitExceeded`,
`quotaExceeded`, `resourceExhausted`) surface as `rate_limited`; permission
denials and unclassifiable bodies surface as the generic provider error. Raw
response bodies, messages, mailbox data, or URLs with IDs are never logged or
exposed over IPC.

### Disposable Mac smoke checklist (Slice 02 prior operator validation)

Run only on the operator-approved disposable-account Mac path:

- Verify fixture is the default, `EMAIL_OS_MODE=gmail` is explicit, and missing
  client ID reports `Not configured` without fixture rows.
- Connect, complete the system-browser OAuth/loopback callback, cancel once, and
  verify cancellation is recoverable; confirm Keychain credentials survive an
  app restart without exposing them.
- Complete bounded initial discovery, inspect plain-text content and unsupported
  content disclosures, and verify archive controls/shortcuts remain absent until
  the separate explicit Slice 03 permission upgrade is enabled.
- Quit, disable network, relaunch, and read cached conversations offline; restore
  network and sync. Change/archive/delete a thread using the external disposable
  Gmail client and confirm catch-up updates the local inbox without skipping the
  expired-cursor recovery path.
- Disconnect and confirm local cache/credentials are cleared while understanding
  that Google authorization itself is not remotely revoked.

No real-account OAuth, Gmail network, or macOS Keychain behavior was tested in the
Linux integration VM. The operator's earlier Slice 01 validation and prior Slice 02
Mac validation are separate gates; neither substitutes for the new Slice 03
consent, mutation, recovery, and external-change checks.

### Mailbox-action validation (Slice 03 still pending on Mac)

Run this only after the separate Slice 02 disposable-account checks, on the
operator-approved disposable Mac account. Keep Gmail read-only until the explicit
upgrade button is chosen. Verify both grant and deny/cancel paths:

- On the read-only account, verify cached reading still works and opening a
  conversation does not mark it read. Request **Enable mailbox actions** only
  after reviewing the broader `gmail.modify` scope disclosure. Confirm the UI
  remains read-only/upgrading until authoritative account status reports a
  verified same-account grant. Deny OAuth and cancel an in-progress upgrade in
  separate runs; each must retain the old read credential, cache and reading
  access without reporting actions enabled. Upgrade cancellation is not
  disconnect and must not revoke a completed Google grant.
- With actions enabled, explicitly archive a conversation, then explicitly
  mark it read and unread. Confirm Activity distinguishes queued, applying,
  confirmed, failed and outcome-unknown; verify ordinary opening does not alter
  read state. Disconnect warning must explain that local pending operations are
  removed but confirmed remote Gmail changes are not undone and Google's grant
  is not revoked.
- Queue an archive while offline, restart, restore network, and verify durable
  Activity/recovery. Interrupted setter dispatch must be reconciled with a GET
  over its exact original message IDs before confirmation; it must not
  automatically POST again. A newer incoming message must not be added to an
  older operation's target snapshot. Use explicit Retry only for a failed or
  outcome-unknown operation and verify it creates a new request ID while
  retaining the old immutable targets; a retry can override the current state.
- Archive enough conversations to exercise the 100-conversation view cap,
  restart, and recover an archived conversation from Activity. The reader must
  identify a retained local recovery snapshot and warn Gmail may have newer
  messages or mailbox changes. Make an external archive/read change in the
  disposable Gmail client, sync, and verify provider facts update without
  erasing a newer pending local intent.

The Slice 03 provider, persistence, bridge and browser behavior is covered with
synthetic HTTP/fake-provider tests only in this VM. This new Mac checkpoint is
not satisfied by the operator's earlier Slice 02 validation; OAuth consent,
Keychain upgrades, native command registration and all Slice 03 scenarios remain
pending operator validation.

### Local drafts and normal close (Slice 04)

Native `list_drafts`, `get_draft`, `create_draft`, `save_draft`, and
`delete_draft` commands use a dedicated `local-drafts/drafts.db` with its own
profile lock and FULL/WAL transactions. The bridge derives account scope from
backend status rather than an account ID supplied by the UI; local drafts do not
require Gmail's `gmail.modify` permission. Disconnect retains local drafts,
but disconnect clears cached account identity, so native list/edit access resumes
after reconnecting the same account. Drafts from another account are never
returned by the selected account's commands.

Draft To/Cc/subject/body text is stored exactly as entered, including incomplete
recipients, whitespace and Unicode. Limits are 16 KiB each for To and Cc, 4 KiB
for subject, and 1 MiB for body; oversized values fail instead of truncating or
normalizing. This is local editor storage, not recipient validation or send
readiness. Revisions start at 1; save/discard use expected-revision checks.
Exact request retries return durable receipts; conflicting reuse of a key is
rejected. Receipts/tombstones do not store body content, and deletes do not let
late saves resurrect a draft. Only a committed receipt is a durable saved label.

Reply is only available for the explicitly selected latest message with complete
current non-retained plaintext and trustworthy metadata. A single From mailbox
is required. Absent Reply-To falls back to From; malformed, empty, group, or
ambiguous Reply-To fails closed. Display names do not expand, aliases and
plus/dot equivalence are not inferred, duplicate mailboxes are removed, and the
account's primary mailbox is excluded. Reply to the account's own latest sent
message is unsupported. A reply starts with empty Cc/body and one `Re:` prefix;
there is no reply-all, Bcc, signature, or automatic quoted text. Legacy cache
rows can use a readonly metadata-only Gmail fetch when online; cached metadata
hits are network-free. If that metadata is unavailable offline, reply preparation
is unavailable, while new-message and existing-draft editing remain local.

Native window Close and normal OS quit pause behind an in-memory
`app_close_requested` request. The UI flushes the current buffer, then completes
only that request after a durable receipt; failure/conflict cancels the request
and leaves the window and buffer open. Requests coalesce, stale IDs are rejected,
and completion without a pending native request cannot close the app. Browser
preview only models this protocol in memory and is never durable. Force quit,
crash, or power loss before a save ACK is not guaranteed to preserve the latest
keystrokes.

### Disposable Mac smoke checklist (Slice 04 pending)

Run only after the existing Slice 02 and Slice 03 operator checkpoints, using a
disposable Mac/profile and no production account:

- Edit recipient, subject, and body immediately before normal window Close and
  Cmd+Q in separate runs; restart and verify exact committed recovery.
- Inject a save failure and a stale-revision conflict during close; verify the
  app stays open, the buffer remains exact, the request is cancelled, and no
  saved label appears without a committed receipt.
- Verify cached/offline, readonly, and auth-expired editing needs no Gmail modify
  grant. Verify a legacy first Reply uses only the readonly metadata enrichment
  path when available.
- Disconnect/reconnect the same account and verify drafts remain on this device;
  switch account and verify no cross-account draft visibility or mutation.
- After reply creation evict/retain the source conversation and verify the
  immutable reply link survives while stale, retained, incomplete, or unsupported
  source preparation fails closed.
- Exercise idempotent retry, duplicate create before metadata reads, delete versus
  late save, and verify no send/outbox/provider-draft side effect.
- Verify fixture native restart recovery and that browser preview continues to
  label its memory-only drafts as non-durable.

Slice 04 synthetic core/UI checks pass in this VM. Native Tauri compile-check
currently stops at the missing `pkg-config`/GTK prerequisites described below;
no OS packages were installed. Native close handling and this Mac checkpoint
remain pending operator validation.

### Safe bulk selection and processing (UX-05)

Conversations can be selected in the Inbox/Done list with `X`, `Shift+J/K`,
Cmd/Ctrl-click, Shift-click ranges and per-row labelled checkboxes, bounded to
100 selected conversations per action (additive ranges; Select all loaded is
disabled with an explanation beyond the bound; selection clears on
context/account changes and survives reader visits with a visible bulk-scope
banner). Shared toolbar, palette and shortcut actions apply to the whole
selection when one exists (group path, even for one row); inline row actions
stay row-scoped, and Reply/open/navigation are never bulk.

A bulk action accepts one durable **operation group**: structure, duplicates,
bounds, request ID, active account and capability are validated before a single
SQLite transaction persists the group header, immutable per-member targets and
preimages, and per-member acceptance results. A gone/unactionable member becomes
a persisted typed rejection, not a fabricated failed provider operation;
all-rejected valid requests get an idempotent receipt and consume no Undo slot.
Same-request replays (including after restart) return the original receipt;
changed payloads are `request_id_conflict`. Archive/unarchive groups work in
fixture and Gmail mode; read/unread groups are Gmail-only, like the single
setters.

`Z` within the 10-second Rust-clock window undoes the latest top-level action,
whether a single or a group. A group Undo makes one durable attempt: queued
members are cancelled, applying/confirmed members are compensated from the
original preimages, and ineligible members (failed, unknown outcome, unknown
prior, already undone, acceptance-rejected) are explicitly skipped with reasons.
Partial results are worded honestly ("Undo accepted for 1 of 2; 1 skipped —
failed"), and per-member failures stay recoverable in Activity regardless of
current list rows. A rejected IPC acceptance is never treated as "nothing
happened": the UI keeps the original request ID and recovers via
`get_operation_group` / replay of the exact original request.

Browser-preview group behavior is modelled by the labelled in-memory fake, which
continues to disclose that it is non-durable; it makes no provider or storage
calls.

#### Disposable Mac smoke checklist (UX-05 pending)

Run only on the operator-approved disposable Mac path, after the Slice 02–04
checkpoints: actual `X`/`Shift+J`/`Shift+K`/Cmd-Shift-click selection and
clear/last-row focus, Escape clearing selection before leaving a context,
bulk Done/read against the fixture or disposable account, `Z` group Undo inside
and outside the window, restart recovery of group receipts and Activity members,
and VoiceOver selection/outcome announcements. Native IPC command registration
is covered only by the bridge tests in this VM; Gmail read-group remote
convergence (BROWSE-18) additionally requires the approved disposable account.

## Native prerequisites and platform limits

The Linux Tauri build needs GTK/WebKitGTK development packages and `pkg-config`,
e.g. on Debian/Ubuntu:

```sh
sudo apt install pkg-config libglib2.0-dev libgtk-3-dev libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev
```

(Also linkable alternatives: `libsoup-3.0-dev` and
`libjavascriptcoregtk-4.1-dev` are WebKitGTK dependencies; macOS uses Xcode
command line tools and WKWebView.) Do not install OS packages as part of a
headless integration check. During UX-05 integration the UX-05 core lane did
install these prerequisites in the Linux integration VM (`pkg-config
libglib2.0-dev librsvg2-dev libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev libsoup-3.0-dev
libjavascriptcoregtk-4.1-dev libgtk-3-dev`), so native compile/bridge gates now
run there; a fresh VM still needs the setup above. Native gates cannot validate
macOS WKWebView/IME, Keychain prompts, system browser
launch, loopback OAuth interaction, or Google TLS behavior.

## Fixture data

Fixture mode uses only synthetic `fixture-account`, `conv-01`…`conv-18` rows,
seeded once; it never resets provider facts or operation history. Gmail mode has a
separate SQLite schema/profile and bounded cache. Neither mode logs subjects,
addresses, bodies, OAuth codes, or credentials. Gmail history catch-up does not
import arbitrary newly observed archived-thread bodies; the disclosed cache is
limited to up to 100 discovered conversations and may omit inbox threads outside
the bounded view.
